raw.quick_summary: The material models ideal projectile motion for a launch and landing at the same height. Initial speed and angle determine the horizontal and vertical components of the launch velocity; gravity then determines the trajectory and flight duration.

key_concepts.explanation: A projectile is launched and lands at the same vertical height under constant gravitational acceleration, with air resistance ignored.
The initial velocity vector is (speed·cos(angle), speed·sin(angle)), separating the launch into horizontal and vertical components.
Horizontal position changes linearly with time: x = speed·cos(angle)·time.
Vertical position follows y = speed·sin(angle)·time − gravity·time²/2, so gravity progressively reduces upward motion.
For a same-height launch and landing, flight ends at time = 2·speed·sin(angle)/gravity.
The model uses a baseline of speed 20 m/s, angle 45°, and gravity 9.8 m/s², with exploration ranges of speed 5–100 m/s, angle 5–85°, and gravity 1–20 m/s².

learning_path.title: From Launch Conditions to Projectile Landing
learning_path.reason: The equations form a natural progression from initial conditions to velocity components, position over time, and the same-height landing condition.

steps.title: Identify the launch conditions
steps.learning_goal: Recognize the roles of speed, angle, and gravity in the model.
steps.explanation: Begin with the baseline values speed = 20 m/s, angle = 45°, and gravity = 9.8 m/s². These parameters define the initial state and can be varied within the stated exploration ranges.
steps.connection_to_previous: This is the starting state for the motion process.

steps.title: Resolve the launch vector
steps.learning_goal: Connect the launch speed and angle to horizontal and vertical velocity components.
steps.explanation: The launch vector is (speed·cos(angle), speed·sin(angle)). The cosine term controls horizontal motion, while the sine term controls initial upward motion.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once the launch conditions are chosen, they determine the initial velocity components.

steps.title: Apply the motion equations
steps.learning_goal: Understand how the two velocity components produce position over time.
steps.explanation: Horizontal position is x = speed·cos(angle)·time. Vertical position is y = speed·sin(angle)·time − gravity·time²/2, with gravity producing the quadratic downward term.
steps.connection_to_previous: The velocity components become the terms that govern position as time passes.

steps.title: Interpret the trajectory
steps.learning_goal: Use x(t) and y(t) together to describe the projectile path.
steps.explanation: Evaluating both equations at the same time gives the projectile's horizontal and vertical location. Changing speed, angle, or gravity changes the resulting trajectory.
steps.connection_to_previous: The position equations combine into the observable trajectory.

steps.title: Determine when the projectile lands
steps.explanation: For a launch and landing at the same height, the nonzero time at which y returns to zero is 2·speed·sin(angle)/gravity.
steps.connection_to_previous: The trajectory reaches the landing condition when its vertical position returns to the launch height.

checkpoint_questions.question: For a fixed launch speed, what does increasing the launch angle primarily do to the initial velocity components?

options.text: It increases the vertical component and decreases the horizontal component.
It decreases the vertical component and increases the horizontal component.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: The components are speed·cos(angle) horizontally and speed·sin(angle) vertically. Over the stated angle range, increasing the angle raises the sine component and lowers the cosine component.

checkpoint_questions.question: According to the vertical-position equation, what is the direct effect of increasing gravity while speed, angle, and time remain fixed?

options.text: The vertical position becomes lower because the downward quadratic term is larger.
The initial vertical velocity becomes larger.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: The vertical position contains −gravity·time²/2, so increasing gravity makes y smaller at a given positive time.

checkpoint_questions.question: If speed and angle are held fixed while gravity increases, what happens to the same-height flight duration?

options.text: It becomes independent of the angle.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: Flight time is 2·speed·sin(angle)/gravity, so increasing gravity increases the denominator and reduces the duration.
